sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Waves for detection and exploration (physics only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain in qualitative terms, how the differences in velocity, absorption and reflection between different types of wave in solids and liquids can be used both for detection and exploration of structures which are hidden from direct observation.

Ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media. The time taken for the reflections to reach a detector can be used to determine how far away such a boundary is. This allows ultrasound waves to be used for both medical and industrial imaging.

Seismic waves are produced by earthquakes. P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. S-waves are transverse, seismic waves. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth’s core.
Echo sounding, using high frequency sound waves is used to detect objects in deep water and measure water depth.
Students should be aware that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to explain in qualitative terms, how the differences in velocity, absorption and reflection ... can be used both for detection and exploration of structures which are hidden from direct observation.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every explanation here is kept qualitative, as the specification demands. Students are asked whether a wave speeds up or slows down, whether it is reflected or transmitted, and whether it is absorbed strongly or weakly. They are never asked for a reflected fraction, an acoustic impedance, an attenuation constant, a refraction angle or any other quantitative treatment of absorption or reflection, and no such quantity appears anywhere in this content.

scopeNotes.statement: The time taken for the reflections to reach a detector can be used to determine how far away such a boundary is.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification supplies no new equation in this section, so none is invented. Distance work uses only the relationship the specification states elsewhere, distance travelled = speed × time, together with the fact this statement itself gives — that what is timed is a reflection, so the pulse has travelled to the boundary and back. Students are asked only for the distance to the boundary, which is half the distance the pulse travels, and for nothing beyond that.

scopeNotes.statement: P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth’s core.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The claim is left exactly as the specification makes it: the two wave types provide evidence for the structure and size of the core. Conclusions are drawn only from the two facts the specification supplies — that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, and that P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. Students are not asked to name internal boundaries or discontinuities, to quote the depth or radius of the core, to explain why a liquid cannot carry a transverse wave, or to state which of the two wave types is faster.

concepts.definition: Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound is ordinary sound — a longitudinal wave that needs a medium — and differs from audible sound only in having a frequency too high for the human ear to detect.

The surface where one material meets a different material, for example soft tissue meeting bone, or one rock layer meeting another. Because the two materials carry the wave differently, a wave arriving at a boundary is changed there rather than passing through unaffected.

When a wave meets a boundary between two different media, part of the wave is reflected back and the rest carries on into the second medium. Ultrasound is partially reflected at every boundary it meets, which is why a single pulse can return several reflections from several depths.

The transfer of energy from a wave to the material it is passing through, so the wave becomes weaker as it travels. Different materials absorb a given wave by different amounts, and how strongly a signal has been weakened is itself information about what the wave has passed through.

The speed at which a wave travels is a property of the wave in a particular material, not of the wave alone. The same wave travels at different speeds in different materials, and it is this difference in velocity at a boundary that produces a reflection and reveals a hidden structure.

Using high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth. A pulse is sent downwards, the time until its echo returns is measured, and the depth is found from that time — remembering that the pulse has travelled down and back.

A wave produced by an earthquake that travels through the Earth. Seismic waves are detected far from the earthquake, and which types arrive where is evidence about the material they have passed through.

A longitudinal seismic wave. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so the times and directions in which they arrive carry information about the material deep inside the Earth.
A transverse seismic wave. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so a region of the Earth that receives no S-waves after an earthquake indicates liquid material somewhere on the path.

The central region of the Earth, which no one has ever seen or sampled. P-waves and S-waves provide the evidence for its structure and its size: S-waves failing to arrive shows liquid material, and the changing speed of P-waves shows where the core begins.

Evidence about something that cannot be observed directly, obtained by measuring what a wave does after passing near or through it. Ultrasound imaging, industrial testing and the study of the Earth's interior all rest on indirect evidence of this kind.

The use of ultrasound to build a picture of a structure hidden from view — an unborn baby or an organ in medicine, a crack or a flaw inside a metal casting in industry. Each reflection detected is turned into the distance to a boundary, and the set of distances becomes the image.

misconceptions.question: Does a wave travel at the same speed in every material?
misconceptions.correct: No. The speed of a wave depends on the material it is travelling through, and it changes when the wave crosses into a different material.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave has one speed of its own, so it travels just as fast through rock, water or metal as it does through air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet a single quoted value for the speed of sound, or for the speed of light, early on and store it as a property of the wave rather than of the wave in one particular medium. Speeds in solids and liquids are rarely quoted beside it.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is the first of the three differences this statement names. It is precisely because the wave travels at a different speed in the hidden material that a boundary reflects part of the wave at all, and the right speed for that medium must be used whenever a time is turned into a distance.

misconceptions.question: When a wave meets a boundary between two materials, is it all reflected or all transmitted?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. Part of the wave is reflected and the rest carries on into the second material — the reflection is partial.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave either bounces off a boundary completely, like a ball off a wall, or passes straight through it unchanged.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reflection is first taught with mirrors, where effectively all the light comes back, and transmission with clear glass, where effectively all of it goes through. Students carry over the two extreme cases and have no picture of a boundary doing both at once.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says ultrasound waves are partially reflected at a boundary. Partial reflection is what makes imaging possible: the reflected part reveals that boundary, and the transmitted part travels on to reveal the next one.

misconceptions.question: If a material absorbs a wave strongly, does it send back a strong reflection?
misconceptions.correct: No. Absorption transfers the wave's energy into the material, so a strongly absorbing material weakens the wave and the signal that comes back is weaker, not stronger.
misconceptions.misconception: Absorption and reflection amount to the same thing — the material takes the wave and sends it back — so a strong absorber gives a strong echo.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words describe something happening to a wave at or inside a material, and students who have not separated the two energy pathways treat them as interchangeable descriptions of the wave being 'stopped'.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists absorption and reflection as separate differences. Reflection sends part of the wave back; absorption removes energy from the wave altogether. A strongly absorbing layer returns a weak signal, and that weakness is itself the clue to what the layer is.

misconceptions.question: Is ultrasound a type of electromagnetic radiation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ultrasound is sound: a longitudinal wave that needs a medium to travel through.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultrasound must be a form of radiation like X-rays, because it is used in hospitals to see inside people.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other hospital imaging method students have heard of uses electromagnetic radiation, so the hospital setting, not the physics, drives the classification. The prefix 'ultra' also echoes 'ultraviolet'.
misconceptions.correction: Ultrasound is defined by its frequency being above the upper limit of human hearing, which only makes sense for sound. It is a mechanical wave, cannot travel through a vacuum, and is not ionising.

misconceptions.question: Is ultrasound sound that is too low in frequency for people to hear?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ultrasound has a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultrasound is sound below the bottom of the human hearing range, like the very low sounds some animals use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that ultrasound lies outside the audible range but not which end of it. Documentary facts about elephants and whales using very low sounds supply a vivid wrong anchor.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Sound below the lower limit is infrasound, which this specification does not require.

misconceptions.question: Is ultrasound simply sound that is too quiet, or too loud, for the ear to detect?
misconceptions.correct: No. What puts ultrasound outside the audible range is its frequency, not how loud or quiet it is.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultrasound is sound at a volume the human ear cannot cope with, so you cannot hear it however hard you listen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday talk about sound is almost entirely about loudness, and students who have not firmly separated amplitude from frequency reach for the property they use daily.
misconceptions.correction: The limits of hearing are limits of frequency. A loud ultrasound wave and a quiet one are both inaudible because the ear cannot respond to that frequency at all.

misconceptions.question: The time until a reflection is detected is measured. Is that the time for a one-way trip?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the time for the pulse to travel to the boundary and back again, so the distance to the boundary is half the distance the pulse travelled.
misconceptions.misconception: The time measured is the time to reach the boundary, so speed × time gives the distance to the boundary directly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply distance travelled = speed × time correctly and then stop, because nothing in the arithmetic itself reminds them that the pulse made a return journey.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the time taken is for the reflections to reach a detector. Speed × time gives the whole there-and-back path; halve it to get the distance to the boundary.

misconceptions.question: Should the halving for a there-and-back journey be applied twice?
misconceptions.correct: No. Halve once, and only once — either halve the time before multiplying, or halve the distance afterwards, but never both.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the pulse goes out and comes back, you halve the time and then halve the answer as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who have been drilled to 'remember to halve' apply the correction as a ritual rather than tracking the journey, so it gets used at both of the available opportunities.
misconceptions.correction: There is one return journey, so there is one factor of two. Halving the time gives the one-way travel time, which already yields the one-way distance; halving that again gives an answer four times too small.

misconceptions.question: Are P-waves transverse and S-waves longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is the other way round. P-waves are longitudinal seismic waves and S-waves are transverse seismic waves.
misconceptions.misconception: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two letters carry no obvious meaning for students, so the pairing is memorised without a hook and is as easily recalled backwards as forwards. Transverse is also the picture students draw for almost every wave.
misconceptions.correction: P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves are transverse. The distinction matters because it is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid, which is the whole basis of the evidence about the core.

misconceptions.question: Are P-waves and S-waves two names for the same kind of wave?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are different types of wave — one longitudinal, one transverse — which is why they behave differently deep inside the Earth.
misconceptions.misconception: P-waves and S-waves are both the same type of seismic wave, differing only in when they arrive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are produced by the same earthquake and recorded on the same trace, so the obvious difference — that one arrives before the other — is taken to be the only difference.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names the type of each separately. If they were the same type they would be stopped by the same things, and there would be no S-wave evidence about the core at all.

misconceptions.question: Does liquid material inside the Earth stop every kind of seismic wave?
misconceptions.correct: No. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, but P-waves can — they simply travel at a different speed in it.
misconceptions.misconception: A liquid blocks seismic waves, so neither P-waves nor S-waves get through the liquid part of the core.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The memorable fact is that something is blocked, and the qualifier 'S-waves only' is the part that drops away. Picturing a liquid as an obstacle also feels intuitive.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, and separately that P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids — which means P-waves do travel through them. That contrast is exactly what makes the evidence work.

misconceptions.question: If no S-waves arrive from beyond the core, is there an empty space inside the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: No. The S-waves are stopped because the material there is liquid, not because there is nothing there.
misconceptions.misconception: Missing S-waves show there is a hollow gap or empty space deep inside the Earth.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that if the waves have stopped there must be nothing to carry them, and 'nothing' is read as empty space rather than as the wrong sort of something.
misconceptions.correction: A liquid is a medium; it carries the longitudinal P-wave perfectly well. What it cannot carry is a transverse wave. Missing S-waves are therefore evidence of liquid, and the region in which they are missing indicates the size of that liquid part.

misconceptions.question: Do S-waves fail to arrive on the far side simply because they have faded away?
misconceptions.correct: No. If distance alone were the reason, the P-waves that travelled just as far would be missing too.
misconceptions.misconception: S-waves are weaker, so they die out before they can reach detectors on the far side of the Earth.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorption over distance is a genuine effect students have met, so it is a ready-made explanation for any wave that fails to arrive, and it needs no thought about the material on the path.
misconceptions.correction: P-waves from the same earthquake do arrive on the far side, so the path length is not the problem. The specification gives the reason directly: S-waves cannot travel through a liquid.

misconceptions.question: Does a P-wave carry the rock along with it as it travels?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rock vibrates back and forth about its own position, along the direction of travel; the wave transfers energy, not material.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave carries the rock along with it, which is why the ground is moved during an earthquake.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Earthquake footage shows ground visibly moving and objects being displaced, which looks like material being carried along. The idea that a wave transfers energy without transferring matter is abstract by comparison.
misconceptions.correction: A P-wave is longitudinal: each part of the rock oscillates back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels, then returns. The energy moves on through the Earth; the rock stays where it is.

misconceptions.question: Could light or radio waves be used instead of sound for echo sounding?
misconceptions.correct: No, not usefully. Light and radio waves are absorbed within a short distance in water, so they cannot reach the sea bed and return.
misconceptions.misconception: Any wave would do the job equally well; sound is used only because it is traditional.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radar and echo sounding are described in the same words — send a pulse, time the echo — so students see the two as interchangeable and never ask what the water does to each wave.
misconceptions.correction: This is exactly the use of absorption the specification asks about. Sound travels a long way through water while light and radio waves do not, so sound is the wave that can carry information back from deep water.

misconceptions.question: Is sound used underwater because sound travels faster than light in water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Light is far faster than sound in water. Sound is used because it is absorbed much less strongly, so it can travel the distance.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound goes faster than light in water, which is why sonar uses sound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know sound travels faster in water than in air and mistakenly extend the comparison to light, helped by the fact that light obviously does not get far down into deep water.
misconceptions.correction: The reason is absorption, not speed. Light and radio waves are absorbed by water over short distances; high frequency sound is not, so it reaches the sea bed and returns.

misconceptions.question: Has anyone drilled down and brought up a sample of the Earth's core?
misconceptions.correct: No. No sample of the core has ever been obtained; everything known about it comes from indirect evidence such as seismic waves.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists have drilled into the core and taken samples, and the seismic evidence just confirms what those samples showed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that rock samples and boreholes exist and do not appreciate the difference in scale between the deepest borehole and the depth of the core.
misconceptions.correction: The specification's point is that these parts of the Earth are not directly observable. Seismic waves provided new evidence about a region no one has ever sampled or seen.

misconceptions.question: If part of the Earth cannot be observed directly, can anything really be known about it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Indirect evidence — measuring what waves do after passing through a region — supports firm and testable conclusions about it.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything you cannot see for yourself is guesswork, so claims about the deep Earth can never be tested.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate evidence with seeing. Indirect measurement is unfamiliar as a form of proof, so a conclusion drawn from it feels like an opinion.
misconceptions.correction: The specification records that seismic waves provided new evidence leading to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable. Predictions made from that evidence are tested against every new earthquake recorded.

mcqs.stem: A survey team sends waves down into the ground to look for a buried rock layer in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens when the waves reach the top of that buried layer?

options.text: The waves carry on downwards at exactly the same speed
options.rationale: A student who treats speed as a property of the wave itself sees no reason for anything to happen at the boundary, and so no reason for the layer to be detectable.

options.text: Part of each wave is reflected back and the rest travels on
options.rationale: A change of velocity at a boundary between two different media produces a partial reflection. The reflected part returns to the detector and reveals the layer; the transmitted part carries on and can reflect from deeper boundaries.

options.text: All of each wave is reflected and none of it travels on
options.rationale: The all-or-nothing picture of reflection taken from mirrors. It would also mean nothing below the layer could ever be surveyed.

options.text: The waves are all absorbed at the top of the buried layer
options.rationale: Absorption is treated as what always happens when a wave meets new material, rather than as a separate effect that weakens a wave as it travels through.

mcqs.stem: Survey waves pass easily through rock layer X but are strongly absorbed by rock layer Y. How does this difference help the team explore ground they cannot see?

options.text: A weak returning signal shows the waves went through layer Y
options.rationale: How much a signal has been weakened is itself information. Waves that come back weak have passed through the strongly absorbing rock, so the strength of each returning signal maps out where each type of rock lies.

options.text: Strong absorption sends back a stronger reflection from layer Y
options.rationale: Absorption and reflection are merged into one idea, so a material that 'takes' the wave strongly is expected to return it strongly as well.

options.text: Layer Y reflects every wave, so nothing returns from below
options.rationale: The all-or-nothing view of a boundary, plus the assumption that a strongly absorbing layer must also be a perfect reflector.

options.text: Both layers return the same signal, so absorption is no use
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think only reflection carries information. The specification names absorption as one of the three differences that make exploration possible.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about ultrasound waves is correct?

options.text: Their frequency is below the lowest frequency a person hears
options.rationale: The student remembers that ultrasound lies outside the audible range but reaches for the wrong end of it.

options.text: They are electromagnetic waves, like the X-rays used in hospitals
options.rationale: Classification driven by the hospital setting rather than the physics: every other imaging method the student knows of uses electromagnetic radiation.

options.text: They are ordinary sound waves that are simply far too quiet to hear
options.rationale: Loudness is substituted for frequency, the property students use to describe sound in everyday life.

options.text: Their frequency is above the highest frequency a person hears
options.rationale: The specification states that ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. They remain sound waves in every other respect.

mcqs.stem: An ultrasound pulse travelling through soft tissue meets a boundary with bone. What happens to the pulse at that boundary?

options.text: All of it bounces back and none enters the bone
options.rationale: Reflection is imagined as total, as with a mirror, so nothing could be imaged beyond the first bone the pulse reaches.

options.text: None of it comes back; it all enters the bone
options.rationale: The other half of the all-or-nothing picture. If nothing came back there would be no signal at the detector at all.

options.text: Part of it is reflected, part carries on
options.rationale: The specification says ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media. The reflected part times that boundary; the rest travels on to the next one.

options.text: It is absorbed there and turned into heat
options.rationale: Absorption is placed at the boundary rather than treated as gradual weakening within a material, and reflection is lost from the picture entirely.

mcqs.stem: An ultrasound pulse leaves a probe on a patient's skin and travels at 1500 m/s. The reflection from a boundary inside the body is detected 0.001 s after the pulse leaves the probe. How far is that boundary from the probe?

options.rationale: Distance travelled = speed × time = 1500 × 0.001 = 1.5 m. That is the there-and-back path, so the boundary is half of it away: 0.75 m.
Speed × time applied correctly but the return journey ignored, so the whole path is reported as the distance to the boundary.
The halving is applied twice — once to the time and again to the distance — giving an answer four times too small.

options.text: 3 m
options.rationale: The return trip is remembered but corrected the wrong way, doubling the path length instead of halving it.

mcqs.stem: A ship measures water depth by echo sounding. It records the time between sending a sound pulse downwards and detecting the echo. How is the depth found from that time?

options.text: Multiply the time by the speed of sound in water
options.rationale: The equation is used correctly but the pulse's return journey is forgotten, so the depth comes out twice as large as it should.

options.text: Divide the speed of sound in water by that time
options.rationale: Chosen by students who recall that the equation links speed, distance and time but rearrange it by guesswork; the answer would not even be a distance.

options.text: Halve the time, multiply by the speed, halve again
options.rationale: The halving is treated as a ritual to be applied wherever it will fit, so the factor of two is used twice for a single return journey.

options.text: Multiply the time by the speed of sound, then halve it
options.rationale: Speed × time gives the whole path the pulse travelled, down to the sea bed and back. The depth is half of that. Halving the time first and then multiplying would be equally correct.

mcqs.stem: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why is sound the wave that is used?

options.text: Sound travels faster through deep sea water than light does
options.rationale: The true fact that sound travels faster in water than in air is over-extended into a comparison with light, which is far faster in water than sound is.

options.text: Water absorbs light and radio waves in a short distance
options.rationale: This is the use of absorption the specification asks students to explain. Light and radio waves do not survive the journey to the sea bed and back; high frequency sound does, so it can carry the information.

options.text: Any wave would work here; sound is just the usual choice
options.rationale: Radar and echo sounding are described in identical language, so the choice of wave looks arbitrary rather than forced by the medium.

options.text: Sound is the only wave the sea bed can reflect back
options.rationale: Reflection is treated as something only sound does, when in fact all waves reflect at a boundary — the problem for light is getting there in the first place.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about P-waves and S-waves is correct?

options.text: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
options.rationale: The pairing is memorised without a hook, so it is recalled the wrong way round about as often as the right way.

options.text: Both P-waves and S-waves are longitudinal waves
options.rationale: The two are treated as one kind of wave differing only in arrival time, which would leave the S-wave evidence about the core unexplained.

options.text: P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves transverse
options.rationale: The specification states that P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves and S-waves are transverse, seismic waves. It is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid.

options.text: Both P-waves and S-waves are transverse waves
options.rationale: The same merging of the two wave types, anchored this time on the transverse picture of a wave that students draw most often.

mcqs.stem: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth record P-waves but no S-waves. What does this indicate about the Earth's core?

options.text: No seismic wave of any kind can pass through the core
options.rationale: The blocking is remembered but not the qualifier. The arriving P-waves in the question contradict this directly.

options.text: There is an empty gap inside the Earth stopping the S-waves
options.rationale: 'Nothing can carry the wave' is read as 'there is nothing there', rather than as material of the wrong kind.

options.text: S-waves are too weak to reach any detector that far away
options.rationale: Fading with distance is a ready explanation for a missing wave, but the P-waves travelled just as far and did arrive.

options.text: Part of the core is liquid: S-waves cannot pass through liquid
options.rationale: The specification states that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. Their absence on the far side, while P-waves still arrive, is the evidence that part of the core is liquid.

mcqs.stem: P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. How does this provide evidence about the Earth's core?

options.text: Where their speed changes shows where the core begins and ends
options.rationale: A change of speed marks a change of material. Tracking where P-waves speed up or slow down, and where they arrive, gives evidence for both the structure and the size of the core.

options.text: P-waves keep one fixed speed, so arrival times give distance only
options.rationale: Speed is treated as a property of the wave rather than of the material, which would make P-waves carry no information about what they passed through.

options.text: P-waves are absorbed by the core, so a shadow shows its size
options.rationale: Absorption is substituted for the change of speed the specification actually states, and the P-waves recorded on the far side show they are not stopped.

options.text: P-waves cannot enter the core, so nothing arrives beyond it
options.rationale: The property of S-waves is transferred to P-waves, contradicting the statement that P-waves travel through liquids at a different speed.

mcqs.stem: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock itself move as the wave passes through it?

options.text: The rock is carried bodily along with the wave as it travels
options.rationale: Earthquake footage of ground and buildings moving suggests that material is being transported rather than energy.

options.text: The rock moves from side to side across the direction of travel
options.rationale: The transverse picture, drawn far more often in lessons, is applied to a wave the specification names as longitudinal.

options.text: The rock vibrates back and forth in the direction of travel
options.rationale: P-waves are longitudinal, so the oscillations of the rock are parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. The rock returns to its position; only energy moves on.

options.text: The rock stays perfectly still while the wave passes
options.rationale: Chosen by students who know a wave transfers energy and not matter, and over-correct into the idea that the medium does not move at all.

mcqs.stem: The study of seismic waves led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable. What did the seismic waves provide?

options.text: Confirmation of what deep drilling had already shown
options.rationale: Boreholes and rock samples are familiar, and their depth is wildly overestimated; no sample of the core has ever been obtained.

options.text: Evidence about material that nobody has seen
options.rationale: The waves pass through regions no one can observe and carry information back out. That indirect evidence is what led to the discoveries about the Earth's interior.

options.text: Ideas about the deep Earth that can never be tested
options.rationale: Evidence is equated with seeing, so a conclusion from indirect measurement is downgraded to guesswork. Every new earthquake tests it again.

options.text: A direct view of the core through the rock above
options.rationale: Imaging is imagined as photography through solid rock, rather than as inference from what a wave does on the way.
